: Five: the āhāraka-pair (āhāraka-śarīra and āhāraka-aṅgopāṅga), nidrā-nidrā, pracalā-pracalā, styānagṛddhi.

t: ** In the apramatta gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?

c.b: ** In the apramatta gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?
: Four: samyaktva-prakṛti and the three inferior saṃhananas.

t: ** In the apūrvakaraṇa gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?

c.b: ** In the apūrvakaraṇa gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?
: Six no-kaṣāyas: hāsya, rati, arati, śoka, bhaya, jugupsā.

t: ** In the anivṛttikaraṇa gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?

c.b: ** In the anivṛttikaraṇa gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?
: Six: the three vedas, and saṃjvalana krodha, māna, māyā.

t: ** In the sūkṣmasāmparāya gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?

c.b: ** In the sūkṣmasāmparāya gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?
: One — sūkṣma lobha (subtle greed).

t: ** In the upaśāntamoha gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?

c.b: ** In the upaśāntamoha gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?
: Two: nārāca and vajra-nārāca saṃhanana.

t: ** In the kṣīṇamoha gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?

c.b: ** In the kṣīṇamoha gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?
: 16: nidrā, pracalā, 5 of jñānāvaraṇa, 4 of darśanāvaraṇa, 5 of antarāya.

t: ** In the sayogakevalī gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?

c.b: ** In the sayogakevalī gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?

: 29: (1) vajra-vṛṣabha-nārāca-saṃhanana, (2) nirmāṇa, (3) sthira, (4) asthira, (5) śubha, (6) aśubha, (7) susvara, (8) duḥsvara, (9) praśasta-vihāyogati, (10) apraśasta-vihāyogati, (11) audārika-śarīra, (12) taijasa-śarīra, (13) kārmaṇa-śarīra, (14) audārika-aṅgopāṅga, (15–24) the 6 saṃsthānas and 4 of varṇādi, (25) agurulaghu, (26) upaghāta, (27) paraghāta, (28) ucchvāsa, (29) pratyeka-śarīra.
Note: According to Ācārya Yativṛṣabhācārya, the fruition of one of sātā or asātā [vedanīya] also ceases here, so according to him there are 30 natures.

t: ** In the ayogakevalī gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?

c.b: ** In the ayogakevalī gunasthana, how many natures cease fruition?

: 13: sātā-asātā-vedanīya, ucca-gotra, manuṣya-āyu, manuṣya-gati, trasa, bādara, pañcendriya-jāti, subhaga, paryāpta, ādeya, yaśaḥkīrti, tīrthaṅkara.
Note: Only one of sātā or asātā [ceases here], since the fruition of one of the two has already ceased at the sayogakevalī stage; hence [effectively] 12.

t: ** What is called naya (a standpoint)?

c.b: ** What is called naya (a standpoint)?

: The knowledge that grasps one attribute (aspect) of an object already properly ascertained through pramāṇa (a valid means of knowledge) is called naya; or, the intention of the knower is called naya.

t: ** What are the main divisions of naya, and what is the basis of each?

c.b: ** What are the main divisions of naya, and what is the basis of each?

: There are two divisions. The basis of niścaya-naya (the essential/real standpoint) is dravyārthika-naya (the substance-viewpoint); the basis of vyavahāra-naya (the practical/conventional standpoint) is paryāyārthika-naya (the modification-viewpoint).

t: ** How many specific divisions of naya are there?

c.b: ** How many specific divisions of naya are there?
: Nine specific divisions: naigama, saṅgraha, vyavahāra, ṛjusūtra, śabda, samabhirūḍha, evambhūta, dravyārthika, and paryāyārthika.

t: ** How many kinds of dravyārthika-naya are there?

c.b: ** How many kinds of dravyārthika-naya are there?
: Three: naigama, saṅgraha, and vyavahāra.

t: ** How many divisions does paryāyārthika-naya have?

c.b: ** How many divisions does paryāyārthika-naya have?
: Four: ṛjusūtra, śabda, samabhirūḍha, evambhūta.

t: ** What is called naigama-naya?

c.b: ** What is called naigama-naya?

: The standpoint that grasps a mere intention (saṅkalpa) regarding an object not yet fully accomplished is naigama-naya. For example, if a woman in the kitchen taking out rice and lentils is asked "what are you doing?" she answers "I am cooking rice" — describing the not-yet-completed act by its intended end.

t: ** What is called saṅgraha-naya?

c.b: ** What is called saṅgraha-naya?
: That which takes as its object an entire collection of things without differentiation is saṅgraha-naya. For example, when one says "jīva" (soul), all souls are meant.

t: ** What is called vyavahāra-naya?

c.b: ** What is called vyavahāra-naya?

: That which treats, by way of distinction, the object grasped [undifferentiated] by saṅgraha-naya is vyavahāra-naya. For example, having grasped "jīva" through saṅgraha-naya, dividing it as far as distinctions go — into saṃsārī (transmigrating) and mukta (liberated), and further dividing saṃsārī into manuṣya, deva, nāraki, tiryañca, and so on — this dividing is called vyavahāra-naya.

t: ** What is called ṛjusūtra-naya?

c.b: ** What is called ṛjusūtra-naya?

: The naya that grasps only objects belonging to the present time, without grasping past or future objects, is called ṛjusūtra-naya. The present is merely a single instant (samaya), and ṛjusūtra-naya takes as its object only the modification (paryāya) of that instant. For example, if one asks a person who has [just] stopped, "Where are you coming from?", the proper answer is "I am not coming from anywhere," because at the very moment the question is asked, the act of coming is not actually occurring.

t: ** What is called śabda-naya?

c.b: ** What is called śabda-naya?

: The naya that takes as its primary object a word established grammatically through a stem (prakṛti) and suffix (pratyaya) is śabda-naya. This naya removes confusion arising from differences of gender, number, tense, case, person, and voice/aspect.

t: ** What is called samabhirūḍha-naya?

c.b: ** What is called samabhirūḍha-naya?

: The naya that takes up mutually-applied (abhirūḍha) synonymous words is samabhirūḍha-naya. In the domain of this naya, even where there is a difference of words, there is no difference of meaning. For example, Śakra, Indra, and Purandara — these three words, being synonyms for devarāja (king of the gods), are all applied to devarāja alone.

t: ** What is called evambhūta-naya?

c.b: ** What is called evambhūta-naya?

: The naya in which the actually-occurring present action is given primary importance is evambhūta-naya. The view that it is proper to apply a word only at the moment the object is actually engaged in the activity that word denotes, and not at any other time, is evambhūta-naya. For example, calling someone a "pūjārī" (worshipper) only while he is actually performing worship.

t: ** How many divisions does paryāya (modification) have? Which are they?

c.b: ** How many divisions does paryāya (modification) have? Which are they?
: Two: artha-paryāya (subtle/momentary modification) and vyañjana-paryāya (durable/manifest modification).

t: ** What is called artha-paryāya?

c.b: ** What is called artha-paryāya?
: The subtle modification that perishes every instant and is beyond the reach of speech is called artha-paryāya.

t: ** What is called vyañjana-paryāya?

c.b: ** What is called vyañjana-paryāya?
: The gross modification that endures for a long time, is expressible in speech, and is perceptible even to a person of limited knowledge, is called vyañjana-paryāya.

t: ** How many kinds of artha-paryāya are there? Name them.

c.b: ** How many kinds of artha-paryāya are there? Name them.
: Two: (1) svabhāva-artha-paryāya (intrinsic momentary modification) and (2) vibhāva-artha-paryāya (extrinsically-conditioned momentary modification).

t: ** In which substances does vibhāva-artha-paryāya occur?

c.b: ** In which substances does vibhāva-artha-paryāya occur?
: Svabhāva-artha-paryāya occurs in all substances (dravyas), but vibhāva-artha-paryāya occurs only in the two substances jīva (soul) and pudgala (matter).

t: ** What is the soul's svabhāva-paryāya?

c.b: ** What is the soul's svabhāva-paryāya?
: In the soul there is the svabhāva-paryāya in the form of jīvatva (the intrinsic nature of sentience), and there is also the vibhāva-paryāya produced by karma.

t: ** How many divisions does vyañjana-paryāya have? Name them.

c.b: ** How many divisions does vyañjana-paryāya have? Name them.
: Four: vibhāva-dravya-vyañjana-paryāya, vibhāva-guṇa-vyañjana-paryāya, svabhāva-dravya-vyañjana-paryāya, and svabhāva-guṇa-vyañjana-paryāya.

t: ** Explain vibhāva-dravya-vyañjana-paryāya with an example.

c.b: ** Explain vibhāva-dravya-vyañjana-paryāya with an example.

: The vyañjana-paryāya of a substance transformed into an extrinsically-conditioned (vibhāva) form is vibhāva-vyañjana-paryāya. For example, states such as being a human or a celestial being are produced by the rise of gati- and āyu-karma, and arise through an overpowering of the soul's own natural state — hence they are vibhāva-paryāya.

t: ** Give an example of vibhāva-guṇa-vyañjana-paryāya.

c.b: ** Give an example of vibhāva-guṇa-vyañjana-paryāya.

: Kumati (wrong sensory knowledge), kuśruta (wrong scriptural knowledge), kuavadhi (wrong clairvoyant knowledge), mati, śruta, avadhi, and manaḥparyaya — these seven kinds of knowledge — and cakṣu-, acakṣu-, and avadhi-darśana — these three kinds of perception — are the soul's vibhāva-guṇa-vyañjana-paryāya.

t: ** Explain svabhāva-dravya-vyañjana-paryāya and svabhāva-guṇa-vyañjana-paryāya with examples.

c.b: ** Explain svabhāva-dravya-vyañjana-paryāya and svabhāva-guṇa-vyañjana-paryāya with examples.

: The siddha-state (a form slightly smaller than the soul's last physical body) is the soul's svabhāva-dravya-vyañjana-paryāya; and the ananta-catuṣṭaya (the fourfold infinitude — infinite knowledge, perception, bliss, and power) is the soul's svabhāva-guṇa-vyañjana-paryāya.

t: ** What are paryāyārthika-naya and dravyārthika-naya?

c.b: ** What are paryāyārthika-naya and dravyārthika-naya?

: From the standpoint of paryāyārthika-naya, substances necessarily arise and perish at every moment; from the standpoint of dravyārthika-naya, they are always of an unperishing and non-arising (eternal) nature.

t: ** What are the two root divisions of naya?

c.b: ** What are the two root divisions of naya?
: Niścaya-naya (or dravyārthika-naya) and vyavahāra-naya (or paryāyārthika-naya). The terms vyavahāra, vikalpa, bheda, and paryāya are all synonyms.

t: ** What is called vyavahāra-naya, and how many divisions does it have? Name them.

c.b: ** What is called vyavahāra-naya, and how many divisions does it have? Name them.

: The standpoint by which a thing is treated through distinction (bheda) and figurative attribution (upacāra) is vyavahāra-naya. It has three divisions: sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya (dealing with a thing's real attributes), asadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya (attributing to a thing what does not truly belong to it), and upacarita-asadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya (figuratively attributing what neither belongs to nor truly resembles the thing).

t: ** What is called niścaya-naya?

c.b: ** What is called niścaya-naya?
: The naya that ascertains a thing through non-distinction (abheda) and literal, non-figurative treatment (anupacāratā) is niścaya-naya.

t: ** What is called sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

c.b: ** What is called sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

: The naya that distinguishes a quality (guṇa) from its possessor (guṇī) on the basis of differences of name, number, defining characteristic, and purpose is sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya. It has two divisions: śuddha-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya (pure) and aśuddha-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya (impure).

t: ** What are śuddha and aśuddha sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

c.b: ** What are śuddha and aśuddha sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

: Stating the distinction between the pure soul (independent of karmic conditioning) as guṇī and its kṣāyika (karma-destruction-born) pure knowledge-quality, or between the siddha soul and the siddha-state, is śuddha-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya; stating the modification/state of an impure (karma-bound) soul is aśuddha-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya.

t: ** What is called asadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

c.b: ** What is called asadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

: Attributing a property properly belonging to one thing onto some other thing is asadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya. It has three divisions: svajātya-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya, vijātya-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya, and svajāti-vijātya-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya. (As printed, these three sub-names retain the term "sadbhūta"; the source text names them this way even though they fall under the asadbhūta category.)

t: ** What is called svajātya-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

c.b: ** What is called svajātya-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

: The naya that attributes to a substance a property arising from its relation with other substances of its own kind (svajātīya) is svajātya-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya. For example, saying "the paramāṇu (atom) is many-space-pointed" — an atom can become many-space-pointed only through combination with other atoms of its own kind.

t: ** What is called vijātya-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

c.b: ** What is called vijātya-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

: The naya that ascribes a property of one kind to a substance of a different kind is vijātya-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya. For example, saying that kṣāyopaśamika mati-jñāna (sensory knowledge arising from the partial destruction-cum-suppression of the corresponding karmas) — itself produced through the kṣayopaśama of the corporeal (mūrtika) mati-jñānāvaraṇa-karma and vīryāntarāya-karma — is itself mūrtika (corporeal): here the quality of corporeality (mūrtitva), which properly belongs to matter (pudgala), is attributed to the soul-quality of knowledge. [The text further notes that] describing the body of a living being as itself the soul is likewise this kind of naya.

t: ** What is called svajāti-vijātya-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

c.b: ** What is called svajāti-vijātya-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

: Since jīva and ajīva are both objects (viṣaya) of knowledge, figuratively attributing the nature of the knowing subject (viṣayī) to the object — and thereby calling the knowable jīva and ajīva themselves "knowledge" — is svajāti-vijātya-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya.

t: ** What is called upacarita-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya? How many divisions does it have?

c.b: ** What is called upacarita-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya? How many divisions does it have?

: That which applies a further figurative attribution on top of an [already] figurative attribution is upacarita-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya. (The source text's list of its three sub-divisions is unclear at this point in the scan; it appears to distinguish a truthfully-figurative, an untruthfully-figurative, and a non-distinguishing figurative form.)

t: ** What is called satya (svajāti) upacarita-asadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

c.b: ** What is called satya (svajāti) upacarita-asadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?
: Saying "[my] son, wife, and so on are mine — I am their master."

t: ** What is called vijātyu (asatya) upacarita-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

c.b: ** What is called vijātyu (asatya) upacarita-sadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?
: Saying "clothes, ornaments, gold, silver, jewels, and so on are mine — I am their owner."

t: ** What is called svajāti-vijātyupacarita-asadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?

c.b: ** What is called svajāti-vijātyupacarita-asadbhūta-vyavahāra-naya?
: Saying "the country, the kingdom, the fort, and so on are mine."
